arguments.name: DIY vs Small Operator Marine Coating Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 DIY boat owners (recruited via marine forums and DIY groups) and 100 small marine operators (recruited via charter boat associations and fishing groups). Each participant views a product description for a Jotun marine coating emphasizing either (a) clear instructions and biofouling protection (DIY version) or (b) reduced downtime and cost savings (small operator version). They are then asked to state their maximum willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and their likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale).
arguments.sample: 200 participants (100 DIY, 100 small operators)
arguments.measure: Average WTP (euros) and purchase intent score for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY version yields higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than small operator version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small operator version yields higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than DIY version.

arguments.decision_rule: If DIY version’s average WTP ≥ €150 and purchase intent ≥ 6/10, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY. If small operator version’s average WTP ≥ €150 and purchase intent ≥ 6/10, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting small operators. If neither version meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed DIY vs Small Operator Marine Coating Test (X1) to empirically compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for the two value propositions before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether there is sufficient demand to justify a differentiated consumer proposition targeting either segment.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B focus on clinics and health clubs and its unknown current reach to individual buyers.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, wellness, or weight management) with a dedicated marketing and distribution strategy.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or bundling with existing clinic/club products without a new consumer brand.
3) Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, retaining royalty income.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser for home use because they value accurate body‑composition data for personal health monitoring.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to track health and weight, especially those with chronic conditions or fitness goals.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Public health messaging links excess body fat to serious diseases, and households already own bathroom scales; a new device that provides precise body‑fat readings would be perceived as a valuable health tool.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a premium price for a consumer‑branded device and sell through retail channels, capturing higher margins than B2B sales.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for home health monitoring devices.
Tanita can adapt its existing technology for consumer use without prohibitive redesign costs.
Retail distribution channels exist for consumer scales in Japan.
predictions: A survey of 500 Japanese adults will show >40% would consider purchasing a home body‑fat analyser at a price of ¥15,000.
Sales of a consumer‑branded version will exceed 1,000 units in the first year if marketed as a health tool.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Health vs. Privacy Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a health‑focused product description (emphasizing accurate body‑fat data for health monitoring) or a privacy‑focused product description (emphasizing discreet home use without public exposure). After viewing, they are asked about purchase intent (binary: "Would you consider buying this device?" ) and willingness to pay (open‑ended).
X1.sample: 500 Japanese adults (aged 20‑65) recruited via an online panel, stratified by gender and age.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average willingness to pay (JPY) for the assigned description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the health‑focused description will show higher purchase intent (>=35%) and higher willingness to pay than those viewing the privacy‑focused description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the privacy‑focused description will show higher purchase intent (>=35%) and higher willingness to pay than those viewing the health‑focused description.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two groups is >=10 percentage points and the group with higher intent corresponds to the theory’s focus (health or privacy), then that theory is supported. If the difference is <10pp, the evidence is inconclusive.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare health‑focused versus privacy‑focused messaging before any product development or marketing spend. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by health awareness or privacy concerns, which is currently unknown from public sources available in 1993.
final.target_customer: Japanese adults aged 20‑65 who currently own a bathroom scale and are interested in personal health monitoring.
final.value_proposition: A stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser positioned as a discreet home health tool that provides accurate body‑fat data for personal health tracking.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €20,000 budget to recruit 500 Japanese adults, stratify by gender and age, and measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under health and privacy messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain because public sources from 1993 do not provide direct evidence of consumer demand for home body‑fat analysers, nor do they address privacy concerns or price sensitivity.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent >=35% and willingness to pay €15,000 for a health‑focused version, proceed with a limited consumer launch.
If the test shows purchase intent >=35% and willingness to pay €12,000 for a privacy‑focused version, explore a privacy‑focused launch.
If the test shows purchase intent <20% for both versions, abandon consumer expansion and focus on B2B growth.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Intent Survey (test X1) to empirically validate demand before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether health‑conscious consumers show sufficient intent to purchase a premium stand‑on analyser, which would justify further development. Until then, maintain the B2B focus and monitor market developments.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B focus on clinics and health clubs and its unknown current reach to individual buyers.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, wellness, or weight management) with a dedicated marketing and distribution strategy.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or bundling with existing clinic/club products without a new consumer brand.
3) Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, retaining royalty income.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers in Japan will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser as a home device to track body composition, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking personal health monitoring; Tanita through premium sales and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of body composition health risks (e.g., heart disease, diabetes), combined with a household culture of using a bathroom scale for health tracking, makes personal body‑fat monitoring attractive.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a consumer‑branded analyser, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and potential subscription services for data analysis.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a stand‑on device compared to lower‑cost alternatives.
The existing scale‑based home measurement culture will transfer to a new body‑fat analyser.
Regulatory acceptance of home bioelectrical impedance analyzers exists in Japan.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑branded stand‑on analyser at a price 20% above existing clinic models, at least 30% of surveyed health‑conscious households will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher in regions with higher obesity rates or strong health‑awareness campaigns.

T2.who_benefits: Consumers seeking measurable fitness improvement; Tanita through volume sales and data‑service partnerships.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in home fitness and weight‑loss programs, combined with the desire for data‑driven results, makes a stand‑on analyser attractive as a tool for tracking progress.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through bulk sales to fitness clubs and retailers, subscription services for data analysis, and premium pricing for consumer‑branded models.
assumptions: Fitness consumers are willing to invest in home devices that provide measurable feedback.
Home fitness market size in Japan was large enough in 1993 to support consumer devices.
Regulatory environment allowed home use of bioelectrical impedance analyzers.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑branded stand‑on analyser at a price 15% above existing clinic models, at least 25% of surveyed fitness‑oriented households will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher in regions with high club membership rates or strong fitness‑awareness campaigns.

X1.name: Consumer Intent Survey for Health‑Conscious vs. Fitness‑Oriented Segments
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of Japanese adults who have expressed interest in health or fitness. Each participant sees a product description of a consumer‑branded stand‑on body‑fat analyser (price set at a 20% premium over clinic models). They then complete a purchase intent scale (1‑10) and indicate whether they would buy it for personal health tracking (T1) or for weight‑loss tracking (T2). The survey also collects demographic data (age, gender, region).
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per segment) recruited via a panel provider, screened for self‑reported health‑consciousness (health‑tracking intent) or fitness‑orientation (weight‑loss tracking intent).
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score for each segment (1‑10).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase intent among health‑conscious participants ≥ 6.5 (30% of sample).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase intent among fitness‑oriented participants ≥ 6.5 (30% of sample).

X1.decision_rule: If either segment meets its intent threshold ≥ 6.5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting that segment. If neither meets the threshold, reject consumer expansion. If both meet the threshold, conduct a secondary test to differentiate the two offers.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Intent Survey (test X1) to empirically validate demand before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether health‑conscious consumers show sufficient intent to purchase a premium stand‑on analyser, which would justify further development. Until then, maintain the B2B focus and monitor market developments.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious Japanese consumers who track body composition for personal health monitoring.
final.value_proposition: A premium, consumer‑branded stand‑on body‑fat analyser sold directly to households, leveraging Tanita’s existing scale‑based home measurement culture and regulatory acceptance of home bioelectrical impedance analyzers.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Intent Survey (test X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 400 participants (200 health‑conscious, 200 fitness‑oriented) at a cost of €15,000.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (health‑conscious demand) and T2 (fitness‑oriented demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer purchase intent for home use.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average purchase intent ≥ 6.5 for either segment, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting that segment.
If neither segment meets the intent threshold, reject consumer expansion and maintain B2B focus.
If both segments meet the threshold, conduct a secondary test to differentiate the two offers.

arguments.name: Consumer Intent Survey for Health‑Conscious vs. Fitness‑Oriented Segments
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of Japanese adults who have expressed interest in health or fitness. Each participant sees a product description of a consumer‑branded stand‑on body‑fat analyser (price set at a 20% premium over clinic models). They then complete a purchase intent scale (1‑10) and indicate whether they would buy it for personal health tracking (T1) or for weight‑loss tracking (T2). The survey also collects demographic data (age, gender, region).
arguments.sample: 400 participants (200 per segment) recruited via a panel provider, screened for self‑reported health‑consciousness (health‑tracking intent) or fitness‑orientation (weight‑loss tracking intent).
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score for each segment (1‑10).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase intent among health‑conscious participants ≥ 6.5 (30% of sample).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase intent among fitness‑oriented participants ≥ 6.5 (30% of sample).

arguments.decision_rule: If either segment meets its intent threshold ≥ 6.5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting that segment. If neither meets the threshold, reject consumer expansion. If both meet the threshold, conduct a secondary test to differentiate the two offers.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Intent Survey (test X1) to empirically validate demand before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether health‑conscious consumers show sufficient intent to purchase a premium stand‑on analyser, which would justify further development. Until then, maintain the B2B focus and monitor market developments.

arguments.target_customer: Health‑conscious Japanese consumers who track body composition for personal health monitoring.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, consumer‑branded stand‑on body‑fat analyser sold directly to households, leveraging Tanita’s existing scale‑based home measurement culture and regulatory acceptance of home bioelectrical impedance analyzers.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Intent Survey (test X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 400 participants (200 health‑conscious, 200 fitness‑oriented) at a cost of €15,000.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 (health‑conscious demand) and T2 (fitness‑oriented demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer purchase intent for home use.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare health‑focused versus fitness‑focused messaging. If the test confirms the predicted purchase intent patterns, proceed to develop a health‑focused consumer version; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus or explore other consumer segments.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B focus on clinics and health clubs and its unknown current reach to individual buyers.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, wellness, or weight management) with a dedicated marketing and distribution strategy.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or bundling with existing clinic/club products without a new consumer brand.
3) Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, retaining royalty income.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious households in Japan will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser as a household health tool, creating demand for a consumer‑branded product.
T1.who_benefits: Japanese households seeking to monitor body composition and health.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of health and body composition, coupled with existing household ownership of bathroom scales, makes a new health‑monitoring device a logical addition.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can sell a branded consumer scale at premium prices, leveraging its existing scale reputation and distribution network.
assumptions: Japanese consumers view body‑fat analysis as valuable health information.
Households are willing to purchase a new health device for home use.
Tanita can adapt its existing B2B technology for consumer packaging and marketing.
predictions: A survey of 500 Japanese households will show >40% indicating intent to purchase a home body‑fat analyser within 12 months.
Sales of a consumer‑branded version will exceed 1,000 units in the first year, generating >¥5 million in revenue.
T1.first_claim: Health‑conscious households in Japan will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser as a household health tool, creating demand for a consumer‑branded product.

T2.claim: Fitness‑oriented consumers will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser as a tool for tracking progress, creating demand for a consumer‑branded product that integrates with home fitness routines.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growth of home fitness and wellness culture, combined with the convenience of a stand‑on device that provides immediate body‑fat data, makes a new health‑monitoring tool attractive for regular use.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can sell a branded consumer scale at premium prices, bundling it with fitness apps or offering subscription services for data analysis, leveraging its existing scale reputation and distribution network.
assumptions: Consumers view body‑fat analysis as a useful metric for fitness progress.
Home fitness market is large enough to support dedicated devices.
Tanita can adapt its B2B technology for consumer‑friendly packaging and marketing.
predictions: A survey of 500 fitness enthusiasts will show >35% indicating intent to purchase a home body‑fat analyser within 12 months.
Sales of a consumer‑branded version will exceed 1,500 units in the first year, generating >¥8 million in revenue.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of Japanese adults aged 25‑65. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) Health‑focused messaging emphasizing body‑fat tracking for overall health and wellness; (B) Fitness‑focused messaging emphasizing immediate body‑fat data for tracking progress and achieving goals. X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age and gender.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑7) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: self‑reported likelihood to recommend to friends.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health‑focused messaging will yield a purchase intent score ≥ 5 and willingness to pay ≥ €150; fitness‑focused messaging will yield a score <4 and willingness to pay <€100.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fitness‑focused messaging will yield a purchase intent score ≥ 5 and willingness to pay ≥ €150; health‑focused messaging will yield a score <4 and willingness to pay <€100.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for health messaging is ≥ 5 and for fitness messaging is <4, proceed with health‑focused consumer proposition. If the opposite pattern holds, proceed with fitness‑focused proposition. If both scores are ≥ 5, conduct a second test to distinguish.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare health‑focused versus fitness‑focused messaging. final.target_customer: Japanese households seeking home health monitoring, particularly those already owning a bathroom scale.
final.value_proposition: A stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyzer positioned as a household health tool, bundled with a consumer‑friendly app or subscription for personalized insights.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline, using the €20,000 budget to recruit 400 participants, collect purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay data, and analyze results.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent ≥ 5 for health messaging and willingness to pay ≥ €150, proceed with T1. If fitness messaging outperforms, reconsider T2. If neither meets thresholds, maintain B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B focus on clinics and health clubs and its unknown current reach to individual buyers.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, wellness, or weight management) with a dedicated marketing and distribution strategy.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or bundling with existing clinic/club products without a new consumer brand.
3) Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, retaining royalty income.

T1.who_benefits: Tanita would benefit by capturing premium sales from consumers who value precise health metrics.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Evidence shows that Japanese households already have bathroom scales and actively track body composition. A stand‑on analyser would provide a faster, more convenient method compared to existing scales.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita could sell the device directly to consumers through retail channels, earning higher margins than B2B sales.

Retail distribution channels exist for consumer electronics in 1993 Japan.
Competitors do not offer comparable stand‑on analysers at comparable accuracy.
predictions: If offered at a price comparable to premium scales, purchase intent among households with existing scales will be higher than among households without scales.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher household ownership of bathroom scales.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would capture value through device sales and subscription fees, potentially higher than a standalone analyser.

predictions: Purchase intent will be higher when the analyser is offered with a fitness subscription than when offered alone.
Conversion rates will be higher in regions with higher fitness club participation.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B focus on clinics and health clubs and its unknown current reach to individual buyers.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, wellness, or weight management) with a dedicated marketing and distribution strategy.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or bundling with existing clinic/club products without a new consumer brand.
3) Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, retaining royalty income.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers in Japan will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for personal health monitoring, and Tanita can capture value by selling a branded consumer device at premium prices.
T1.who_benefits: Japanese consumers seeking to track body composition and health status; Tanita benefits from direct consumer sales and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of health risks linked to body fat (as shown by household scale ownership) creates demand for accurate, convenient home measurement. A trusted brand like Tanita signals quality and reduces perceived risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells a consumer‑branded scale at a price above generic models, retaining margin and building brand equity.
assumptions: Japanese consumers are willing to pay a premium for health‑related home devices.
Tanita’s existing B2B reputation transfers to consumer trust.
Distribution channels (retail or direct) are feasible in 1993.
predictions: In a test offering a Tanita home scale at a price 20% above generic competitors, purchase intent among health‑conscious households will be at least 15% higher than for a generic device.
Surveyed users will cite reliability and ease of use as primary reasons for choosing Tanita.

Tanita can partner with or build a credible health coaching platform.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Subscription Bundle
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 Japanese adults (100 health‑conscious, 100 general) via panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two offer groups: (A) Premium home scale (price 20% above generic competitors) with no subscription; (B) Same premium scale bundled with a 3‑month health‑coaching subscription (monthly fee €15). Both offers include a brief product description and a "Purchase Now" button. Track whether participants click the button and, if they do, collect self‑reported primary reason (e.g.,
X1.sample: 200 Japanese adults (100 health‑conscious, 100 general) recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: clicked "Purchase Now") and primary reason (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health‑conscious participants will show higher purchase intent for the premium scale alone (group A) than for the bundled scale (group B).
prediction_by_theory.T2: All participants will show higher purchase intent for the bundled scale (group B) than for the premium scale alone (group A).

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between groups A and B is at least 10 percentage points in favor of the bundled offer (group B), conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is at least 10 percentage points in favor of the premium offer (group A), conclude evidence supports T1. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish theories.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, pricing, or willingness to pay for a branded home body-fat analyser. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent for a premium home scale versus a bundled scale. If the test shows a 10‑percentage‑point or greater advantage for the bundled offer, reconsider T2; otherwise, maintain the current B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Japanese consumers seeking personal health monitoring, particularly health‑conscious households.
final.value_proposition: A Tanita‑branded home body‑fat analyser sold at a premium price, delivering reliable personal health data and brand trust, with optional subscription for personalized coaching.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 budget to recruit 200 participants and test the two offers.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence from 1993. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a 10‑percentage‑point or greater advantage for the bundled offer, shift focus to T2 and consider subscription‑based pricing.
If the test shows a 10‑percentage‑point or greater advantage for the premium scale, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health‑conscious households.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 Japanese adults (100 health‑conscious, 100 general) via panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two offer groups: (A) Premium home scale (price 20% above generic competitors) with no subscription; (B) Same premium scale bundled with a 3‑month health‑coaching subscription (monthly fee €15). arguments.sample: 200 Japanese adults (100 health‑conscious, 100 general) recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: clicked "Purchase Now") and primary reason (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health‑conscious participants will show higher purchase intent for the premium scale alone (group A) than for the bundled scale (group B).
prediction_by_theory.T2: All participants will show higher purchase intent for the bundled scale (group B) than for the premium scale alone (group A).

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between groups A and B is at least 10 percentage points in favor of the bundled offer (group B), conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is at least 10 percentage points in favor of the premium offer (group A), conclude evidence supports T1. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish theories.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility within a €20,000 test budget and 12‑week timeframe.
Any recommendation must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
The test budget and timeframe are analyst assumptions; actual company resources are unknown.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand into adjacent B2B markets (e.g., leisure boats, aviation maintenance) without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they perceive them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and will purchase them at a price that reflects reliability and regulatory compliance.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, campers, paddlers) gain confidence in emergency response; ACR gains revenue from premium-priced consumer devices.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: After the FCC legalized PLBs in 2002 and required mandatory registration, users will see a beacon as a required safety item for high-risk activities, leading them to buy rather than rent.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers at higher margins than B2B rentals, and can bundle the beacon with safety kits or insurance, creating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that meets regulatory standards.
The outdoor recreation market is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Distribution channels exist to reach individual buyers.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz beacon at a price above $200.
Sales of a consumer-focused beacon will be positively correlated with the number of outdoor recreation events promoted in media.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they perceive them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and will purchase them at a price that reflects reliability and regulatory compliance.

T2.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they perceive them as a status symbol and a way to signal expertise, and will purchase them to demonstrate preparedness and to network with fellow users.
T2.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation users gain social recognition and a sense of belonging; ACR gains revenue from premium-priced consumer devices and from accessories that signal expertise.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: After the FCC legalized PLBs and media coverage highlighted successful rescues, users will view beacons as a badge of preparedness, leading them to buy to show off their knowledge and to connect with peers.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell limited-edition or branded accessories, offer membership programs for beacon owners, and charge higher prices for devices that signal exclusivity.
assumptions: Consumers value social signaling and status within outdoor communities.
Media coverage of PLB rescues creates a positive public image that enhances perceived value.
Distribution channels exist to reach outdoor enthusiasts directly.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz beacon at a price above $200, motivated by status and networking.
Sales will be higher in regions with active outdoor media coverage and established outdoor communities.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, paddlers) who engage in remote activities and prioritize safety.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon positioned as a safety-essential tool for remote travel, sold at a premium price that reflects regulatory compliance and reliability, bundled with safety kits or insurance to create recurring revenue.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 test budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness-to-pay data for safety-focused and status-focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity in 2002. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10 percentage-point advantage for the safety-focused version, proceed with a consumer-focused product. If the status-focused version wins, reconsider the status-driven proposition.
If neither version achieves a ≥10 percentage-point advantage, abandon consumer expansion and focus on B2B markets.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility within a €20,000 test budget and 12‑week timeframe.
Any recommendation must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
The test budget and timeframe are analyst assumptions; actual company resources are unknown.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand into adjacent B2B markets (e.g., leisure boats, aviation maintenance) without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers at higher margins than B2B rentals, and can bundle the beacon with safety kits or insurance, creating recurring revenue.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, paddlers) who engage in remote activities and prioritize safety.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon positioned as a safety-essential tool for remote travel, sold at a premium price that reflects regulatory compliance and reliability, bundled with safety kits or insurance to create recurring revenue.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 test budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness-to-pay data for safety-focused and status-focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity in 2002. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10 percentage-point advantage for the safety-focused version, proceed with a consumer-focused product. If the status-focused version wins, reconsider the status-driven proposition.
If neither version achieves a ≥10 percentage-point advantage, abandon consumer expansion and focus on B2B markets.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.

arguments.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon positioned as a safety-essential tool for remote travel, sold at a premium price that reflects regulatory compliance and reliability, bundled with safety kits or insurance to create recurring revenue.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 test budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness-to-pay data for safety-focused and status-focused messaging.
arguments.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity in 2002. The test will resolve this uncertainty.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.

final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 test budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness-to-pay data for safety-focused and status-focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity in 2002. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10 percentage-point advantage for the safety-focused version, proceed with a consumer-focused product. If the status-focused version wins, reconsider the status-driven proposition.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility within a €20,000 test budget and 12‑week timeframe.
Any recommendation must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
The test budget and timeframe are analyst assumptions; actual company resources are unknown.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand into adjacent B2B markets (e.g., leisure boats, aviation maintenance) without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, campers, paddlers) gain confidence in emergency response; ACR gains revenue from premium-priced consumer devices.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: After the FCC legalized PLBs in 2002 and required mandatory registration, users will see a beacon as a required safety item for high-risk activities, leading them to buy rather than rent.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers at higher margins than B2B rentals, and can bundle the beacon with safety kits or insurance, creating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that meets regulatory standards.
The outdoor recreation market is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Distribution channels exist to reach individual buyers.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz beacon at a price above $200.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell limited-edition or branded accessories, offer membership programs for beacon owners, and charge higher prices for devices that signal exclusivity.
assumptions: Consumers value social signaling and status within outdoor communities.
Media coverage of PLB rescues creates a positive public image that enhances perceived value.
Distribution channels exist to reach outdoor enthusiasts directly.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz beacon at a price above $200, motivated by status and networking.
Sales will be higher in regions with active outdoor media coverage and established outdoor communities.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer motivations, regulatory necessity, or purchase behavior for outdoor recreation. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, paddlers) who engage in remote activities and are aware of regulatory requirements for distress signaling.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon positioned as a safety-essential tool for remote travel, meeting regulatory compliance and FCC approval, sold at a premium price to capture higher margins and recurring revenue from accessories and insurance.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness-to-pay data for safety-focused and status-focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (safety-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence from 2002 sources. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10 percentage-point higher purchase intent for the safety version, we would proceed with a safety-focused consumer product. If the status version wins, we would explore a status-driven proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference, we would maintain the B2B focus and monitor market developments.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they perceive them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and will purchase them at a price that reflects reliability and regulatory compliance.
arguments.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, campers, paddlers) gain confidence in emergency response; ACR gains revenue from premium-priced consumer devices.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: After the FCC legalized PLBs in 2002 and required mandatory registration, users will see a beacon as a required safety item for high-risk activities, leading them to buy rather than rent.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers at higher margins than B2B rentals, and can bundle the beacon with safety kits or insurance, creating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that meets regulatory standards.
The outdoor recreation market is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Distribution channels exist to reach individual buyers.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz beacon at a price above $200.
Sales of a consumer-focused beacon will be positively correlated with the number of outdoor recreation events promoted in media.

predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz beacon at a price above $200, motivated by status and networking.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility within a €20,000 test budget and 12‑week timeframe.
Any recommendation must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
The test budget and timeframe are analyst assumptions; actual company resources are unknown.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand into adjacent B2B markets (e.g., leisure boats, aviation maintenance) without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Safety Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. Participants indicate purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" or "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (continuous, €).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. and Canadian outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and activity frequency.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate "Would buy" for each version. Secondary: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the safety-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the safety version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher proportion of participants will indicate "Would buy" when shown the status-focused version, and average WTP will be higher for the status version.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion who would buy the safety version exceeds the proportion who would buy the status version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status version exceeds the safety version by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude the evidence is insufficient to distinguish the theories.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer motivations, regulatory necessity, or purchase behavior for outdoor recreation. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare safety-focused versus status-focused messaging before any expansion decision. The test will determine whether consumer demand is driven by regulatory necessity (T1) or social signaling (T2). Until then, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor market developments.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, paddlers) who engage in remote activities and are aware of regulatory requirements for distress signaling.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon positioned as a safety-essential tool for remote travel, meeting regulatory compliance and FCC approval, sold at a premium price to capture higher margins and recurring revenue from accessories and insurance.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness-to-pay data for safety-focused and status-focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (safety-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence from 2002 sources. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10 percentage-point higher purchase intent for the safety version, we would proceed with a safety-focused consumer product. If the status version wins, we would explore a status-driven proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference, we would maintain the B2B focus and monitor market developments.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility within a €20,000 test budget and 12‑week timeframe.
Any recommendation must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
The test budget and timeframe are analyst assumptions; actual company resources are unknown.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand into adjacent B2B markets (e.g., leisure boats, aviation maintenance) without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a product description for a 406 MHz PLB: (1) safety-focused, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency distress, and FCC approval; (2) status-focused, emphasizing social signaling, expert recognition, and limited-edition branding. X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product description and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a neutral description emphasizing practicality, reliability, and cost savings; (B) a status-focused description emphasizing modern, well-kept image, prestige, and social signaling. After reading the description, participants are asked: (1) on a 0‑100 scale how much they would pay for the tractor (WTP); (2) whether they would purchase the tractor even without prior tractor ownership (demand).
X1.sample: 400 households (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, screened for having a small garden (under 0.5 acre) and living in a market served by John Deere dealers.
X1.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and proportion of participants who indicate purchase intent without prior ownership.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the neutral condition (convenience) compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition (status) compared to the neutral condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the neutral condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 15% (or €200), we conclude evidence supports T1. If the average WTP in the status condition exceeds the neutral condition by at least 15%, we conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is less than 15%, we conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish the theories.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare demand for convenience versus status messaging. If the test confirms a ≥15% higher willingness-to-pay for the neutral description, proceed to develop a differentiated convenience-focused consumer line; otherwise, maintain the current business model.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US who are considering a lawn and garden tractor for yard work.
final.value_proposition: A Deere-branded lawn and garden tractor positioned as a practical, reliable tool that saves time and money, sold through existing dealer network, leveraging Deere’s reputation for durability.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €18,000 budget to recruit 400 households, collect willingness-to-pay and purchase intent data, and analyze results against the 15% threshold.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (convenience demand) and T2 (status demand) remain uncertain due to limited public evidence from 1962. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥15% higher willingness-to-pay for the status description, we would shift focus to a lifestyle-focused proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference between descriptions, we would maintain the current business model.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Status Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized product description and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a neutral description emphasizing practicality, reliability, and cost savings; (B) a status-focused description emphasizing modern, well-kept image, prestige, and social signaling. After reading the description, participants are asked: (1) on a 0‑100 scale how much they would pay for the tractor (WTP); (2) whether they would purchase the tractor even without prior tractor ownership (demand).
arguments.sample: 400 households (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, screened for having a small garden (under 0.5 acre) and living in a market served by John Deere dealers.
arguments.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and proportion of participants who indicate purchase intent without prior ownership.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the neutral condition (convenience) compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition (status) compared to the neutral condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the neutral condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 15% (or €200), we conclude evidence supports T1. If the average WTP in the status condition exceeds the neutral condition by at least 15%, we conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is less than 15%, we conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish the theories.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product description and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a neutral description emphasizing practicality, reliability, and cost savings; (B) a status-focused description emphasizing modern, well-kept image, prestige, and social signaling. After reading the description, participants are asked: (1) on a 0‑100 scale how much they would pay for the tractor (WTP); (2) whether they would purchase the tractor even without prior tractor ownership (demand).
X1.sample: 400 households (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, screened for having a small garden (under 0.5 acre) and living in a market served by John Deere dealers.
X1.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and proportion of participants who indicate purchase intent without prior ownership.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the neutral condition (convenience) compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition (status) compared to the neutral condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the neutral condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 15% (or €200), we conclude evidence supports T1. If the average WTP in the status condition exceeds the neutral condition by at least 15%, we conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is less than 15%, we conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish the theories.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare demand for convenience versus status messaging. If the test confirms a ≥15% higher willingness-to-pay for the neutral description, proceed to develop a differentiated convenience-focused consumer line; otherwise, maintain the current business model.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US who are considering a lawn and garden tractor for yard work.
final.value_proposition: A Deere-branded lawn and garden tractor positioned as a practical, reliable tool that saves time and money, sold through existing dealer network, leveraging Deere’s reputation for durability.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €18,000 budget to recruit 400 households, collect willingness-to-pay and purchase intent data, and analyze results against the 15% threshold.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (convenience demand) and T2 (status demand) remain uncertain due to limited public evidence from 1962. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥15% higher willingness-to-pay for the status description, we would shift focus to a lifestyle-focused proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference between descriptions, we would maintain the current business model.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product description and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a neutral description emphasizing practicality, reliability, and cost savings; (B) a status-focused description emphasizing modern, well-kept image, prestige, and social signaling. After reading the description, participants are asked: (1) on a 0‑100 scale how much they would pay for the tractor (WTP); (2) whether they would purchase the tractor even without prior tractor ownership (demand).
X1.sample: 400 households (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, screened for having a small garden (under 0.5 acre) and living in a market served by John Deere dealers.
X1.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and proportion of participants who indicate purchase intent without prior ownership.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the neutral condition (convenience) compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition (status) compared to the neutral condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the neutral condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 15% (or €200), we conclude evidence supports T1. If the average WTP in the status condition exceeds the neutral condition by at least 15%, we conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is less than 15%, we conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish the theories.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Status Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized product description and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the Midwest/Northeast US. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a neutral description emphasizing practicality, reliability, and cost savings; (B) a status-focused description emphasizing modern, well-kept image, prestige, and social signaling. After reading the description, participants are asked: (1) on a 0‑100 scale how much they would pay for the tractor (WTP); (2) whether they would purchase the tractor even without prior tractor ownership (demand).
arguments.sample: 400 households (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, screened for having a small garden (under 0.5 acre) and living in a market served by John Deere dealers.
arguments.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and proportion of participants who indicate purchase intent without prior ownership.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the neutral condition (convenience) compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition (status) compared to the neutral condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the neutral condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 15% (or €200), we conclude evidence supports T1. If the average WTP in the status condition exceeds the neutral condition by at least 15%, we conclude evidence supports T2. If the difference is less than 15%, we conclude insufficient evidence to distinguish the theories.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare demand for convenience versus status messaging. If the test confirms a ≥15% higher willingness-to-pay for the neutral description, proceed to develop a differentiated convenience-focused consumer line; otherwise, maintain the current business model.
